questions.enonce_markdown:
Describe the following DBMS terms:

(a) Attribute. (1 mark)

(b) Entity. (1 mark)

(c) Redundancy. (1 mark)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(a) Attribute (1 mark).** A property or characteristic of an entity; in a table it is a column (field), for example Name, Date_of_birth or Address of a Student entity.

**(b) Entity (1 mark).** A person, object, place or event about which data are stored in the database (for example Student, Teacher, Course); each entity becomes a table and each occurrence of it is a record (row).

**(c) Redundancy (1 mark).** The unnecessary repetition of the same data in several places in a database; it wastes storage space and can produce inconsistencies (the same item has different values in different places) when one copy is changed and the others are not.

questions.enonce_markdown: Describe one data validation method and one data verification method. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Data validation (1 mark).** Validation is an automatic check by the computer that the data entered are reasonable and acceptable, though not necessarily correct. Example, a *range check*: the program rejects an age of 250 or a mark of 120 out of 100 because the value is outside the allowed range (0 to 120, or 0 to 100). Other methods: type check, presence check, length check, format check.

**Data verification (1 mark).** Verification checks that the data entered are the same as the original source, that is, that no error was made in copying them. Example, *double entry*: the data are typed twice (often by two operators) and the computer compares the two entries and reports any difference. Another method is a visual check (proof-reading) of the screen against the source document.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Briefly explain the following database structures:

(a) Relational database. (2 marks)

(b) Hierarchical database. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(a) Relational database (2 marks).** The data are stored in several tables (relations) made of rows (records) and columns (attributes). Each table has a primary key, and the tables are linked to one another by foreign keys (for example the StudentID of a Student table is repeated in an Enrolment table), so that data are not repeated and can be combined with queries (SQL). Examples: MySQL, Oracle, MS Access.

**(b) Hierarchical database (2 marks).** The data are organised as a tree: a single root record at the top with parent records and child records below it; each child has only one parent, and a parent may have many children (one-to-many relationships only). To reach a record one must follow the path from the root down. Examples: a company organisation chart, the folders and files of a computer.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) Explain the difference between synchronous and asynchronous data transmission modes. (4 marks)

(c) Differentiate between serial and parallel transmission. Illustrate the two transmission methods by a diagram. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(a) Synchronous and asynchronous transmission (4 marks).**

- **Asynchronous transmission:** the data are sent one character (one byte) at a time. Each character is framed by a *start bit* and one or two *stop bits*, which tell the receiver where the character begins and ends, so the sender and the receiver do not need a common clock and the gaps between characters can be of any length. It is simple and cheap, but the extra bits make it slow and less efficient (about 20 % overhead for 8 data bits). Example: a keyboard sending to a computer.
- **Synchronous transmission:** the data are sent as a continuous block (frame) of many characters, at regular intervals controlled by a clock shared by the sender and the receiver (synchronisation characters at the start of the block keep them in step). There are no start and stop bits for each character, so there is less overhead and the transmission is faster and more efficient, but the equipment is more complex and expensive. Example: data transfer between computers on a network, or between a computer and a server at high speed.

**(c) Serial and parallel transmission (2 marks).**

- **Serial transmission:** the bits of a character are sent one after the other along a single wire (channel). It needs only one line, so it is cheaper and works over long distances (USB, Ethernet), but it is slower for the same clock speed.
- **Parallel transmission:** several bits (for example 8) are sent at the same time, each on its own wire. It is faster over short distances (the bus inside a computer, an old printer cable), but it needs many wires, is more expensive, and over long distances the bits arrive at different times (skew) and interfere with each other.

```
SERIAL (one wire)
Sender  ---- 1 0 1 1 0 0 1 0 ---->  Receiver
        (bits follow one another on the same line)

PARALLEL (eight wires)
Sender  ---- bit 1 ---->  Receiver
        ---- bit 0 ---->
        ---- bit 1 ---->
        ---- bit 1 ---->
        ---- bit 0 ---->
        ---- bit 0 ---->
        ---- bit 1 ---->
        ---- bit 0 ---->
        (the 8 bits of a byte travel together)
```
